title: Promoting active learning with ChatGPT: A constructivist approach in Sri Lankan higher education
extended_summary:
This paper addresses how ChatGPT can be used to shift a traditional, didactic learning environment toward active, constructivist learning in a resource-constrained higher education setting. The central question is not whether ChatGPT improves test scores, but what teaching and learning strategies make it useful for promoting active learning, social interaction, contextual learning, scaffolding, and reflective thinking.

The study was conducted in a Sri Lankan university over 12 weeks with 43 undergraduate students in a project management course. The intervention combined pre-class materials, short instructor-led introductions, group discussions, ChatGPT-supported case studies, and post-class sample answers generated with ChatGPT. The instructor also guided students in using ChatGPT responsibly, including warnings about hallucinations and the need to verify information. Data came from 15 semi-structured student interviews and thematic analysis, so the study is qualitative and based primarily on learner perceptions.

The paper identifies 16 strategies across five constructivist themes and argues that ChatGPT can help educators create more interactive, learner-centered experiences without additional resources. It concludes that AI can support personalized feedback, collaboration, and reflection, while the educator’s role shifts toward collaborator and guide. The author also notes that the approach was especially feasible in a low-resource setting, though broader generalizability remains limited.
quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative action-research study with semi-structured interviews and thematic analysis, not a controlled efficacy design. It provides useful implementation evidence but does not meet stronger causal credibility criteria.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports clearly positive but non-quantified impacts on engagement, collaboration, and understanding in one higher-education class. Because no effect sizes or objective outcome gains are reported, the magnitude of impact is unclear.

interventions.use_case: Using ChatGPT as a virtual tutor and collaborator in a higher-education project management course to generate case studies, support group discussions, provide instant feedback, answer questions, and scaffold active learning

finding.finding_summary: Students reported that ChatGPT-supported activities increased critical thinking, collaboration, reflective thinking, and problem-solving in a 12-week action-research intervention with 43 undergraduates in Sri Lanka. The paper is qualitative and does not report standardized effect sizes, but it describes stronger engagement in group discussion, more confident participation, and improved ability to apply concepts through the AI-supported case-study and discussion activities.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes about critical thinking, collaboration, reflective thinking, and problem-solving during ChatGPT-supported active learning

finding.finding_summary: The intervention was associated with higher student engagement, motivation, and confidence in participating in class and group work. Students described ChatGPT as making learning more engaging and less intimidating, but the study provides qualitative evidence only and no numeric effect size.
finding.measure: Semi-structured interview themes on engagement, motivation, confidence, and participation

finding.finding_summary: The paper focuses on project management learning in higher education and reports that ChatGPT helped students understand course concepts through contextualized case studies and immediate feedback. Evidence is based on qualitative student interviews from a 12-week intervention rather than objective achievement testing, so no effect size is reported.
finding.measure: Qualitative perceptions of understanding and application of project management concepts
